draft.title: Evaluating a scientific claim
card: A claim is only as strong as the evidence behind it. Ask what was measured and whether the evidence actually supports the claim.
Look at the study. A larger sample and a fair test, with variables controlled and measurements done carefully, give more trustworthy results.
Look for repeats. If other scientists run their own studies and find the same result, confidence in the claim grows.
Check who made or paid for the study. A funder with something to gain is a reason to look more closely at the method. It does not prove the result is wrong.
draft.remember: Strong claims have good evidence, a well-run study, repeated results and a source you can trust.

a.q: A website claims a new drink improves memory. Which finding would make you trust the claim most?
opts: Several separate studies found the same memory gain
One study of 20 people found a memory gain
The drink's maker says the gain is large
Many people online say they feel sharper
a.why: Separate studies that find the same result show the effect can be repeated. A single small study could be a fluke, and the maker's word and online opinions are not controlled evidence.
a.clue: Which finding has been checked by more than one team?

b.q: A battery company pays a lab to test its batteries. The lab reports they last longer than rivals. What is the best response?
opts: Check how the test was run and look for other tests
Reject the result because the company paid for it
Accept the result because a lab ran the test
Accept it because the batteries are sold widely
b.why: Funding by a company is a reason to check the method and look for independent tests of the same thing. Rejecting the result outright is tempting, but funding alone does not show the result is wrong.
b.clue: A funder with something to gain calls for a closer look, not an automatic verdict.
